description: AutoModerator feature-level metrics, scraped from automoderator-bot's /metrics (services/automoderator-bot/src/lib/metrics.ts).

panels.title: Cases filed by action ($window)
panels.description: A case is the permanent record; the panel below counts the Discord calls. They differ on purpose -- a WARN files a case and touches Discord only to DM, and a ban the audit observer noticed files a case for a call this bot never made.

panels.title: Cases filed by source ($window)
panels.description: What decided each case. `command` is a moderator typing one; everything else decided on its own. `observer` is a manual ban, unban or kick taken in Discord's own UI that this bot only recorded, so it is the one source that means nothing here acted.

panels.title: Punishments carried out ($window)
panels.description: The six member-affecting actions only. `delete`, `dm`, `message` and `webhook` go through the same executor seam but are deletion, notification and logging traffic that would bury this -- they are on the rows below. Incremented only once Discord accepts the call, so a rejected one lands on `automoderator_discord_errors_total` and never here.

panels.title: Filter hits by filter ($window)
panels.description: Hits, not punishments: a hit with no policy configured and one a bypass role let off both land here. That is the point -- "this rule is catching far more than you thought" is a question about hits, and the punishment panel above already answers the other one. `words` is a native Discord AutoMod hit; the other three are this bot's own runners.

panels.title: Native AutoMod intake ($window)
panels.description: `AUTO_MODERATION_ACTION_EXECUTION` as it arrives, counted before deduplication. Flat zero while guilds have banword policies configured is this port's most likely silent failure: either no guild has native keyword rules or the `AutoModerationExecution` intent is not granted. `action_type` is Discord's own enum -- 1 block, 2 alert, 3 timeout, 4 block member interaction. `matched=false` is an event carrying no `matched_keyword`, which is the assumption feature 01's whole design rests on.

panels.title: Features applied ($window)
panels.description: Feature-level intake, so "is feature N working in prod" is answerable without reading logs. `applied` means the feature did its thing -- for a log, that the embed was built and handed to the dispatcher, not that Discord accepted it. Delivery is the log webhook panel below.

panels.title: Features skipped ($window)
panels.description: The expected outcome for most traffic: an exempt channel, a bypass role, immunity, a message that was never cached, a guild with nothing configured for the rule that fired. Read it next to `applied` rather than alone -- `filters` only ever reports `skipped` and `failed`, because a hit is attributed to the runner that caught it.

panels.title: Feature failures ($window)
panels.description: Should sit flat at zero. Every point here is an exception a feature entry point caught, counted and logged -- the guild configured something and it did not happen.

panels.title: Report queue transitions ($window)
panels.description: `state` is the transition that happened, not the row's current value: `filed` opens a report, `joined` is a second reporter agreeing with an existing one, `dismissed`/`actioned` resolve one and `restored` takes a dismissal back. **Intake is bot-only** -- DM reports are filed by `services/api`, which has its own registry, so they never reach `filed` or `joined` here, while their resolutions do because those go through this bot's card buttons. `dismissed + actioned` exceeding `filed` is that, not double counting.

panels.title: Filed vs resolved ($window)
panels.description: Intake climbing with resolution flat is a queue filling up that nobody is reading, which is the failure this counter exists for. The two lines are not expected to match even in a healthy week -- see the panel to the left for why.

panels.title: Scheduler runs ($window)
panels.description: The three sweeps on the timer -- there is no task table to draw `type` from, because the case row is the schedule. There is deliberately no third "gave up" result: a failing expiry is retried every tick forever, since abandoning one turns a temporary ban into a permanent one. So `failed` climbing with no `ok` behind it is a stuck row, not a lost one.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, type) (rate(automoderator_scheduler_lag_seconds_bucket[$window]))) and on (type) (sum by (type) (increase(automoderator_scheduler_lag_seconds_count[$window])) > 0)

panels.title: Scheduler lag, p95 ($window)
panels.description: `run_at` to actually running. Climbing means tempbans are not expiring, which surfaces as "why is this user still banned" long before anyone thinks to look at a bot. Buckets run out to an hour so a wedged loop and a healthy one do not both read as `+Inf`. Only `expiry` observes this -- the other two sweeps have no due time to be late against. The `and on (type)` guard drops a series with no observations in the window rather than drawing NaN.

panels.title: Log webhook deliveries ($window)
panels.description: `failed` is usually a deleted log channel rather than an outage: the dispatcher self-heals by dropping the row, so a spike here is followed by *silence* on that `log_type` until somebody reconfigures the channel. The silence is the part worth noticing.

panels.title: Message cache hit rate ($window)
panels.description: Whether a delete or an edit arrived with the original still in redis to describe. **Retention pressure, not intent health** -- a falling rate means deletes are reaching further back than the cache keeps, past `MESSAGE_CACHE_TTL_MS` or past `MESSAGE_CACHE_MAX_PER_CHANNEL` in a channel busy enough to have evicted its own recent history. Both are answered by those two constants. Guarded ratio -- the `> 0` sits around the denominator so a window with no deletes drops the series rather than drawing a confident zero.

panels.title: Discord responses by status ($window)
panels.description: Written by one RESTEvents.Response listener in @chatsift/bot-core's createBotRest, so it covers every Discord call this bot makes. Counts Discord's *answers*: a connection-level failure (ECONNRESET, timeout) throws before the event fires and is not here.

panels.title: Failing routes ($window)
panels.description: `route` is the rate-limit bucket route, with every snowflake already replaced by `:id`.

panels.title: Rejected actions by route class ($window)
panels.description: The subset of the failures above that were *doing something to somebody*, bucketed by what: `member` is a ban, kick, timeout or role change, `message` a delete or a card post, `user` a DM, `webhook` a log. The split matters because the fix differs -- a 403 on `member` is role hierarchy in one guild, a 404 on `webhook` is a deleted log channel. Bot-process only: `services/api` writes some of the same objects from the dashboard with its own registry, so a dashboard-initiated write Discord refuses is invisible here.

Gateway shards the whole cluster is running, summed over the one target per replica that `dns_sd` gives this job. Below the bot's shard count means a replica is missing and part of the guild list is receiving no gateway events at all.
panels.title: Cluster shard coverage

panels.description: Scraping targets currently answering. Should match what `./compose ps automoderator-bot` shows; scaling is opt-in and stays at one until `AUTOMODERATOR_SHARDS_PER_REPLICA` is set.
panels.title: Replicas up
Shards owned per replica
panels.description: One series per container. A replica reading above `AUTOMODERATOR_SHARDS_PER_REPLICA` is covering for a missing peer. Coverage cannot change while a process lives -- @discordjs/ws cannot reshard a live manager -- so every step here is a restart, and a series that ends without another starting is a replica that never came back.

panels.title: Replica slot per container
panels.description: Which slot each replica claimed from the Redis index lease. **Two containers reading the same slot is the failure to watch for**: a lease that expired or was evicted lets a second replica claim an index that is already taken, and both then run the same gateway shards. Redis holds these leases under a TTL, which is why this deployment runs with no `maxmemory` -- a `volatile-*` eviction policy would evict exactly the keys that make this safe.

list.description: Lookback window every increase/rate on this dashboard is computed over. Bot feature counters are far lower-volume than the API's per-route metrics -- most fire a handful of times an hour across the whole fleet -- so Prometheus's ~5m default leaves nearly every series at zero, which makes any ratio a 0/0 NaN and any histogram_quantile NaN too. Widen this if panels still show an em dash; narrow it to chase a short-lived spike.
list.label: Window
